title: Nussbaum
keyWorks: The Fragility of Goodness: Luck and Ethics in Greek Tragedy and Philosophy (1986)
Love's Knowledge: Essays on Philosophy and Literature (1990)
The Therapy of Desire: Theory and Practice in Hellenistic Ethics (1994)
Upheavals of Thought: The Intelligence of Emotions (2001)
Hiding from Humanity: Disgust, Shame, and the Law (2004)
Anger and Forgiveness: Resentment, Generosity, Justice (2016)
The Monarchy of Fear: A Philosopher Looks at Our Political Crisis (2018)
summary: Martha Nussbaum (b. 1947) is an American philosopher who works on ancient thought, ethics and law. She shows that a good human life is inevitably vulnerable: it depends on luck, on other people and on the body. Together with the economist Amartya Sen, Nussbaum developed the “capabilities approach” — an account of the basic capabilities every person needs in order to live a life of dignity — and she has written extensively about how emotions shape our personal and public lives.
onEmotions: Nussbaum's central idea is that emotions are not blind forces but “judgments of value.” Every emotion contains a thought that something not fully within our control matters greatly to our life: grief says “I have lost someone infinitely dear to me,” fear says “something I care about is under threat.” That is why emotions have their own intelligence — they can be understood and examined. Nussbaum argues against the Stoics, who wanted to be free of emotion: for her, emotions are an acknowledgment of our vulnerability and our attachments, without which life would be poorer. At the same time she carefully analyzes the dangerous emotions — disgust, primitive shame, anger's wish for payback, and fear — and shows how they grow out of the wish not to be vulnerable.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is exhausting, and there is nothing shameful about it. Martha Nussbaum holds that emotions are not blind pushes but “judgments of value”: each one contains the thought that something important to your life lies outside your control. Anxiety is a blurred form of fear: you sense that something dear to you is under threat, but you can't quite say what it is or where the danger will come from. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum writes that fear is our earliest emotion: it comes from the helplessness of infancy, and adults still carry its trace. Seen this way, anxiety is not a malfunction but a sign that you have something worth protecting. Once you can name that value, anxiety usually becomes more concrete and quieter.
anxiety.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm anxious because I care about…” — and name one specific thing or person.

fear.text: Fear is an honest response to what could hurt you. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum calls it the most ancient emotion: an infant depends entirely on others and cannot protect itself, and fear arises earlier than love or compassion. She notices something particular about fear: it narrows the world down to “me” and “my safety,” and it tends to become a “monarch” — to rule over the other feelings, turning into anger, disgust or envy. Nussbaum doesn't suggest erasing fear: it often points to a real vulnerability. But she advises against handing it all the power, and suggests giving a voice to what widens the world — hope, love, trust, working on something together. You can be afraid and still not let fear decide for you.
fear.practice: Name your fear in one sentence, and next to it write what else is in you right now besides fear: love, curiosity, hope. Let fear have a neighbor.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and it doesn't need to be hurried. For Nussbaum, emotions are judgments of value, and sadness contains the thought: “Something mattered to me, and it is gone or there is less of it.” The Stoics, whom Nussbaum studied closely in The Therapy of Desire, considered such judgments a mistake: the wise person should not depend on what is beyond their control. Nussbaum respects the Stoics but disagrees with them here: the people, work and places that don't depend on us really do matter. That is why sadness often tells the truth — about your attachment and about your capacity to value things. To accept it is to admit that you live not in a fortress but among things that can be loved and lost.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: “What value is this sadness telling me about?” Write down the answer without judging it.

grief.text: Grief is one of the hardest things a person goes through. Nussbaum opens Upheavals of Thought (2001) with her own grief — the death of her mother. For her, grief is not a meaningless storm but a judgment of enormous force: a person who was part of the very structure of your life is gone. That is why grief is so all-encompassing: it touches not a single thought but the whole picture of what matters to you. Nussbaum shows that grief changes as these judgments are gradually rebuilt: the bond with the one who died does not disappear, but finds a different place within your life. To grieve is to acknowledge the worth of the one you lost. It is not weakness or illness, but a form of love that goes on.
grief.practice: Write down one thing this person brought into your life that has stayed with you.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and the pain is about something important. Together with the economist Amartya Sen, Nussbaum developed the “capabilities approach”: there are basic human capabilities without which a life cannot be fully human. One of them is “affiliation” — being able to live with and toward others, to have close relationships and to have the social bases of self-respect. Seen this way, loneliness is not a personal flaw but a signal that one of the central human needs has no outlet right now. Nussbaum stresses that such capabilities depend not only on us but also on how the society around us is arranged. Your loneliness is not a verdict on your ability to love, but a reminder that you are made for connection.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person you felt good with, even just once. Write them a couple of lines — even if you don't send them right away.

anger.text: Anger often points to a real injustice, and it shouldn't be ignored. In Anger and Forgiveness (2016), drawing on Aristotle, Nussbaum distinguishes two parts of anger: the pain of having been wrongfully harmed, and the wish for “payback” — for the wrongdoer to suffer. The first part is justified. The second Nussbaum disputes: another's suffering doesn't undo the harm. She calls this “the road of payback,” and when anger turns into a concern with who is now “on top,” “the road of status.” The way out she sees is “Transition-Anger”: acknowledging that something unacceptable has happened, and turning toward the future — to what can be changed. Your anger is a legitimate signal, and it can be directed where it actually helps.
anger.practice: Put into words what exactly hurt you, and then just one thing: what could actually make things better in the future?

quote.text: How outrageous! Something should be done about this.
quote.author: Martha Nussbaum
quote.source: Anger and Forgiveness (2016) — the formula of “Transition-Anger”

shame.text: Everyone knows shame, and it shows that being a decent person matters to you. In Hiding from Humanity (2004), Nussbaum describes “primitive shame”: its roots lie in early childhood, when a child wants to be all-powerful and perfect, and discovers instead that it is small, dependent and imperfect. This shame at our very human limitations comes back again and again later on. Nussbaum distinguishes it from “constructive” shame, which helps us strive toward ideals. Primitive shame demands the impossible — to be invulnerable. Once you recognize it, you can tell yourself: my needs and mistakes don't make me worse than others; they make me human, like everyone else.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: “Am I ashamed of a specific act, or of being imperfect at all?” If it's the second, remind yourself that this is how everyone is made.

guilt.text: Guilt is heavy, but it shows that you care how your actions affect others. Drawing on the psychoanalyst Melanie Klein, Nussbaum sees guilt as a mature feeling: it arises when we realize we have hurt someone we love and want to make it right. In Hiding from Humanity she contrasts guilt with shame: shame says “I am bad through and through,” while guilt says “I did something bad,” and so guilt opens the way to “reparation” — to making amends. At the same time, in Anger and Forgiveness Nussbaum warns against anger at oneself, against the wish to punish oneself: self-punishment doesn't repair the harm. Useful guilt looks forward — toward care and restoring the connection.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: is there one small action that could set things right even a little, or show that you care?

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant to admit, but everyone feels it. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum describes envy as a painful emotion focused on other people's goods and on comparison with oneself: others have what I don't, and that hurts. She believes envy is often rooted in fear and insecurity, and that envy sees the world as a zero-sum game: if someone has won, then I have lost. Nussbaum distinguishes envy from “emulation” — the wish to become like the other. Looked at closely, envy shows what you value. You can take that knowledge for yourself and leave the hostility toward the other person aside.
envy.practice: Finish the sentence: “I envy them because I also want…” What part of that could you move toward, even with a small step?

emptiness.text: Emptiness is a quiet but heavy state, and it's hard to explain to others. For Nussbaum, emotions are judgments about what matters in your life. From this point of view, you could say that emptiness is a time when those judgments seem to have fallen silent: things are there, but their value can't be felt. In The Therapy of Desire, Nussbaum argues against the Stoic ideal of “apatheia” — freedom from the passions — and shows that a life without attachments becomes poorer. Yet in The Fragility of Goodness she also writes about how vulnerable attachments are. Perhaps emptiness is not your absence but a pause for breath after valuing things has hurt. Your values haven't disappeared; they need time and gentleness to respond again.
emptiness.practice: Today, notice one small thing that stirred a response in you, even for a second: a smell, a sound, someone's word. Just note it, without asking for more.

confusion.text: Feeling lost is natural when life takes an unexpected turn. Nussbaum compares emotions to “geological upheavals”: they make the inner landscape uneven, and the old maps stop working. Following Aristotle, she holds that practical wisdom is not a set of ready-made rules but “perception” — the ability to see the particulars of a concrete situation attentively. In Love's Knowledge (1990), Nussbaum shows that literature teaches exactly this: to see what is complex without simplifying it. From this point of view, being lost is not a failure but an honest admission that the situation is more complicated than ready-made answers. The way out is not a quick conclusion but patient attention to detail: what is really happening here, and what matters to me.
confusion.practice: Describe the situation as a scene from a novel: who is there, what they feel, what is at stake. What details hadn't you noticed before?

quote.text: Emotions shape the landscape of our mental and social lives. Like the “geological upheavals” a traveler might discover in a landscape where yesterday was only flat ground, they mark our lives as uneven, uncertain, and prone to reversal.
quote.author: Martha Nussbaum

fatigue.text: Fatigue is not laziness or a flaw of character. Nussbaum keeps reminding us that a human being is a “needy animal”: we have bodies that need rest, sleep and care. In Hiding from Humanity she shows how often people are ashamed of this bodily vulnerability and dream of being tireless, like machines. Her list of central human capabilities includes both bodily health and “play” — being able to laugh, to rest and to enjoy recreational activities. This is not a pleasant extra to life but part of it. From this point of view, fatigue is the body's legitimate message about its limits, not a reason to reproach yourself. Letting yourself rest means recognizing yourself as a living being, not a tool.
fatigue.practice: Ask yourself: which kind of rest — sleep, play, quiet, company — do you need most right now? Set aside at least ten minutes for it.

boredom.text: Boredom can be agonizing, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. Nussbaum wrote very little about boredom directly, but her list of central human capabilities includes “senses, imagination, and thought,” as well as “play.” From this point of view, you could say that boredom is a signal: these capacities have nothing to do right now. In Love's Knowledge, Nussbaum speaks of “attentive perception” — the ability to notice the fine details of people and situations, as Henry James's characters do. Such attention can bring to life even what seemed all too familiar. Boredom is not a verdict on you or on the world; it can be an invitation to look more closely, or to let yourself play.
boredom.practice: Choose one object nearby and describe it in as much detail as a writer would: its color, texture, history. What new thing did you notice?

joy.text: Joy is worth welcoming with your whole heart. For Nussbaum, joy is a judgment that something truly valuable has happened in your life. In The Fragility of Goodness (1986) she shows that many valuable things — love, friendship, the success of a shared undertaking — depend on luck and on other people, and are therefore fragile. But for Nussbaum this fragility doesn't cancel their value; often it is part of it: we rejoice in what might not have happened at all. So there's no need to hold joy back for fear of losing it, or to diminish it by saying “it won't last.” You can simply admit: right now I'm lucky, and this is worth living fully.
joy.practice: Pause for a minute: what exactly is making you glad, and who or what had a part in it? Say it to yourself in words.

love.text: Love is one of the most important and most vulnerable feelings. Nussbaum devoted a large part of Upheavals of Thought and the collection Love's Knowledge to it. She argues with the philosophers who wanted to “raise” love from a particular person to something general and safe, as in Plato's “ladder of love.” What Nussbaum values is love for a particular, irreplaceable person — with all their peculiarities, their separateness and their freedom. She believes love also brings knowledge: through it we see the other and ourselves more clearly. Such love inevitably makes us vulnerable, but that vulnerability is not a mistake — it is the price of being open. Let yourself love without demanding guarantees from love.
love.practice: Name three traits of someone you love that belong only to them. Notice how that feels.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling worth staying with. From Nussbaum's point of view, it contains a judgment: someone else has done something valuable for my life. It is an acknowledgment of dependence on others — the very thing many philosophical traditions, the Stoics for example, wanted to free us from. Nussbaum, on the contrary, considers dependence part of a normal human life: we are not self-sufficient fortresses but beings who need others. True, in Anger and Forgiveness she warns that in close relationships it's better not to keep “score” — neither of hurts nor of favors. Living gratitude is not a debt to be repaid, but the joy of not being alone and of knowing that goodness really does happen.
gratitude.practice: Think of one person thanks to whom your life is better now. If you can, tell them so today.

hope.text: Hope is a feeling worth trusting, and one you can grow. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum writes that hope and fear are twins: both arise when the outcome of something important is uncertain. But fear shrinks and retreats, while hope widens the world and moves us to act. Following Kant, Nussbaum speaks of hope as a practical stance: not a forecast that everything will be fine, but a choice to live and act as if the good is possible. She suggests sustaining hope through “practices” — art, friendship, taking part in shared work. Your hope is not naivety but a way of holding on to what you care about in the midst of uncertainty.
hope.practice: Write down one small thing you could do today “on behalf of” what you hope for.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a bittersweet feeling, and it has its own wisdom. From Nussbaum's point of view, you could say that nostalgia is a judgment about the value of the past: something there meant a great deal to you. In The Fragility of Goodness she shows that many of life's goods depend on circumstances and cannot last forever — but that doesn't make them any less real. Nostalgia recognizes this: the good was there, and it was fragile. At the same time, Nussbaum cautioned against idealizing a past that seems more secure than it really was. A gentle nostalgia doesn't pull you backward; it reminds you that you know how to value things — and that ability stays with you in the present too.
nostalgia.practice: Recall what exactly made that time valuable. Is there anything of it you could bring back into your life now, even a little?

craving.text: Craving can be very strong, and in itself it doesn't make you a bad person. In The Therapy of Desire (1994), Nussbaum shows how the Hellenistic philosophers — Epicurus, Lucretius, the Stoics — saw philosophy as medicine for the soul. Their important discovery, which Nussbaum shares, is that desires contain beliefs. Epicurus distinguished natural desires from “empty” ones, which are inflated by false thoughts like “I can't bear it without this.” From this point of view, you can do more than endure a craving — you can calmly examine it: what belief is speaking in it, what does it promise? A craving usually rises like a wave and then subsides. While you are examining it, you are no longer simply the one carrying it out.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, write down the thought that speaks in it (“I need…, because…”) and note the time. Then watch how the strength of the wave changes.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure, and shame doesn't help here. In The Therapy of Desire, Nussbaum describes the Hellenistic “medical model” of philosophy: a good philosopher, like a good doctor, pays attention to the particular person, their history and circumstances, rather than lecturing them. Her capabilities approach includes “practical reason” — being able to plan one's own life — and addiction narrows exactly this capability. Nussbaum stresses that a person's capabilities also depend on their surroundings and on the support they receive. From this point of view, getting free of addiction is not a matter of willpower alone, but a gradual regaining of your freedom, in which the help of others belongs.
addiction.practice: Think about whether there is a person or a community where you'd be understood without judgment — for example, a mutual-help group. Just write down who that could be.

hangover.text: The morning after can be hard on both body and soul. Nussbaum wrote a lot about how people are ashamed of their bodily nature, and in Hiding from Humanity she distinguished two feelings that often come at such moments. Guilt says: “I did something I regret” — and suggests setting something right. “Primitive shame” says: “I'm no good at all” — and only paralyzes. From this point of view, it helps to separate one from the other: acknowledge specific actions, if there were any, and don't pass a verdict on yourself as a whole. Your body is asking for care right now, not punishment. Being kind to yourself is not letting yourself off the hook; it's what makes it possible to sort things out calmly later.
hangover.practice: Do one simple caring thing for your body right now: water, fresh air, quiet. The sorting out can wait until later.

euphoria.text: A high, when everything seems possible, is a vivid experience, and you can value it. Nussbaum compares emotions to “geological upheavals” that change the landscape of a life, and in euphoria that landscape suddenly becomes vast and full of light. In her view, intense joy contains a judgment that something valuable has come closer. It's worth noticing what exactly lifted you so high: a success, a meeting, an idea? In The Fragility of Goodness, Nussbaum reminds us that much of what is good is fragile and depends on circumstances — but that is no reason to give up joy, only a reason to live it attentively. Savor this moment, remember what it is about, and let it become part of your story.
euphoria.practice: Write down what exactly lifted you up and what you see more clearly now than usual. You can reread it on other days.

crash.text: The drop after a high can feel like falling from a great height, and it really is hard. Nussbaum writes that emotions make our lives “uneven, uncertain, and prone to reversal” — this is not a glitch but a feature of a being who cares about things. From her point of view, you could say that in a crash your judgments of value shift: what seemed huge and close a moment ago suddenly seems distant or unimportant. But a new judgment that arrives in a moment of exhaustion is not necessarily truer than the old one. Neither the rise nor the fall passes a final verdict on your life. The crash is part of the landscape you are walking through, not the end of it, and you can wait it out while being gentle with yourself.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “This is a crash, and it's a state, not a final result.” Do one simple thing for your body — water, food, a few minutes of rest.

panic.text: Panic is genuinely frightening: your body seems to slip out of control, and it feels as though it will never end. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum writes that fear is our most ancient emotion, dating from the time when an infant is helpless and wholly dependent on others. In panic this ancient fear rises at full strength, bypassing the arguments of reason. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. In Nussbaum's view, the counterweight to fear is support and presence — what an adult's arms once gave the infant. For a grown-up, that support can come from your own body: the floor under your feet, slow breathing, the objects around you named out loud.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and feel the support. Take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath, and silently name five things you can see.

dread.text: A sense of impending disaster is hard to bear, especially when it has no clear cause. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum observes that fear isolates: it drives a person inward, into concern for their own safety, and the world becomes narrow and dark. She also writes that fear often grows in solitude and weakens alongside others — in trust, in shared work. From this point of view, you could say that a heavy foreboding is not a prophecy but the voice of a very old fear that speaks louder when you are alone. Nussbaum suggests setting hope against fear — not as certainty of a good outcome, but as a readiness to hold on to what is dear. You don't have to stay with this feeling alone.
dread.practice: Say out loud, or write to someone you trust: “I'm feeling anxious and heavy right now.” One sentence is already a step out of isolation.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out on something important is understandable: life offers more than you can hold. In The Fragility of Goodness, reading Greek tragedy, Nussbaum shows that there are many values and they aren't always compatible: in choosing one good, we inevitably lose another. She calls this “the tragic question” and believes that an honest life acknowledges such losses rather than pretending you can have everything. From this point of view, your fear of missing out is not greed but a vision of how much of value there is in the world. The pain of what you didn't choose is natural. But a life in which you are fully present in one thing is richer than a life in which you are mentally everywhere and truly nowhere.
fomo.practice: Choose one thing you are doing today and tell yourself: “Right now, I'm choosing this.” Notice how your attention changes.

sleepless.text: A sleepless night wears you out, and thoughts in the dark feel heavier than they do by day. From Nussbaum's point of view, you could say that at night what she calls “the monarchy of fear” grows sharper: we are alone, the world has gone quiet, and the ancient sense of helplessness returns. The judgments that seem so indisputable at three in the morning are born of fatigue and loneliness, not of clear sight. Nussbaum reminds us that we are bodily, needy beings, and that is no reason to reproach ourselves. Insomnia says nothing bad about you, and you don't have to settle everything that worries you tonight. You can simply take care of yourself, the way you would care for someone close who couldn't fall asleep.
sleepless.practice: Place a hand on your chest or belly and take a few slow out-breaths. Tell yourself: “Night thoughts are not final. I'll look again in the morning.”

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply because it strikes at trust — one of the most valuable things we have. In The Fragility of Goodness, Nussbaum shows that much in a good life depends on other people, and is therefore inevitably vulnerable. To trust is not naivety but the condition of friendship and love. In Anger and Forgiveness she writes that in close relationships, behind anger at a betrayal there is often grief: you have lost not only a person but also what you believed in. Dreams of payback won't bring back what was lost, while grief, if you allow it to be, frees you over time. Your pain is evidence that you knew how to trust. That ability was not a mistake, and you don't need to lose it because of one person.
betrayal.practice: Try to name what exactly you lost besides the person: faith, plans, a picture of the future. Let yourself grieve for it.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing, and even very loving people feel it. Nussbaum reads Proust closely — he explored jealousy in more detail than anyone: his narrator wants to possess his beloved completely, to know her every thought — and still cannot. In Upheavals of Thought, Nussbaum shows that jealousy mixes love, fear of loss and the wish to control the other. The problem is that the other person is separate and free, and that is often exactly what makes them loved. In her view, jealousy is a signal of how much this person means to you. You can acknowledge it without turning it into an attempt at control, and ask yourself what fear it is speaking of.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm afraid that…” Then ask yourself: what do I need right now to feel safe — and can I say it directly?

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is a heavy burden, and it's understandable that it arose: you were treated unjustly. In Anger and Forgiveness, Nussbaum describes how resentment clings to a fantasy of “payback”: it seems that if the wrongdoer suffers, the balance will be restored. She calls this thought a kind of “magical thinking”: another's suffering does not undo the harm done to you. Nussbaum also criticizes “transactional” forgiveness, in which the other is required to show humiliating contrition. Instead she proposes the path of “transition”: acknowledge that something unacceptable happened, and turn your attention to the future — to your own life and to what can be changed. Letting go of resentment doesn't mean excusing the wrongdoer; it means no longer handing them your strength.
resentment.practice: Ask yourself: “If the person who wronged me punished themselves tomorrow, what would actually change in my life?” Write down what you truly need.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains there is, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. In Love's Knowledge, Nussbaum examines an episode from Proust: the narrator, sure that he no longer loves, discovers his love only at the moment his beloved leaves — through pain. For Nussbaum this is an important lesson: suffering is itself a form of knowledge of how much a person meant to you. In Upheavals of Thought she shows that such a loss is like grief: it takes time for your judgments of value to be rebuilt and for this person to take a different place in your life. The pain is not proof that you were wrong to love. It proves that you know how to love.
heartbreak.practice: Write one sentence about what you have learned about yourself thanks to this love. That knowledge will remain yours.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're “in the wrong place” and are about to be exposed is familiar to many capable people. From Nussbaum's point of view, you could say that behind it there is often the “primitive shame” she describes in Hiding from Humanity: a childhood demand on yourself to be perfect and all-powerful. Against that demand, any normal uncertainty looks like proof of fraud. Nussbaum stresses that all people are limited, need others and learn as they go — and that those who look flawless are also hiding their vulnerability. You don't have to be perfect to have a right to your place. Being a person who is growing is not a forgery; it's the ordinary human norm.
impostor.practice: Write down three things you have already done well, and next to each, what you learned along the way. Notice: learning is not the same as deceiving.

self_hatred.text: If you are treating yourself with hatred right now, that is very painful, and you don't deserve such cruelty. In Hiding from Humanity, Nussbaum describes “primitive shame” — the demand on yourself to be perfect, invulnerable, without needs or weaknesses. When this impossible demand isn't met, an inner voice passes a verdict on the whole person. But that verdict is not the truth about you; it is an echo of an unreachable ideal. Nussbaum speaks of compassion as the recognition that a person is suffering undeservedly and that their suffering matters. From this point of view, you could say that compassion has every right to be turned toward yourself as well. You deserve at least the kindness you would give a friend in the same pain.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine a close friend telling you these words about themselves. What would you say to them? Say it to yourself, even in a whisper.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is one of the hardest feelings: you want to change something, but you can't. In The Fragility of Goodness, Nussbaum shows that the Greeks understood this well: much in life depends on tyche — chance, luck, what is beyond our control. The heroes of tragedy, good people, suffer not through their own fault but because of circumstances. For Nussbaum this is not a reason for despair but an honest picture of human life: we are not all-powerful, and no one is. Your helplessness is not proof of weakness but an encounter with this shared truth. In it you can find support in other people: where one person is powerless, together we can often do more.
helplessness.practice: Divide a sheet of paper into two columns: “not in my power” and “at least a little in my power.” In the second column, choose one small action.

procrastination.text: Putting things off is not laziness, and there are often feelings behind it that are hard to notice. Nussbaum didn't write about procrastination directly, but her idea that emotions contain judgments helps. From her point of view, you can ask: what judgment is hiding behind the delay? Sometimes it's fear of being judged, and the “primitive shame” of Hiding from Humanity — the demand to do it perfectly right away, or better not at all. Sometimes it's a conflict of values: this task matters to you, and so does rest, and so does something else. Nussbaum values attentive “perception” of the concrete situation over general rules like “just pull yourself together.” If you understand which feeling is holding you back, starting becomes easier: you are working with the cause, not treating yourself as an enemy.
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: “What am I afraid of in this task?” Then take the smallest step — for five minutes, with no demand to do it well.

uprooted.text: The feeling of having been torn up by the roots is a real loss, even if the change was one you chose. For Nussbaum, emotions are tied to the particular: to specific people, places, sounds and habits that were part of the structure of your life. That is why losing a familiar environment is experienced as grief, not just as inconvenience. Her list of central capabilities includes “affiliation” and “control over one's environment” — and when these are disrupted, life objectively becomes harder. In Political Emotions (2013), Nussbaum writes about how strongly particular songs, places and stories bind us to the world. Your longing for your roots speaks of how deeply you can form attachments — and that ability will help you put down roots again.
uprooted.practice: Name one small, specific thing from your old place that you miss. Could you find or create something like it here?

overload.text: Overload is when there's too much of everything at once, and it drains you. From Nussbaum's point of view, you could say that every request, task and piece of news contains the judgment “this matters,” and when there are too many such judgments, attention simply can't cope. In The Fragility of Goodness she writes about “the tragic question”: sometimes different important things cannot all be done at once, and it is more honest to admit this than to blame yourself for lacking strength. Nussbaum values attentive “perception” of the particular — and attention is finite. Her list of capabilities includes both “play” and rest. From this point of view, overload is not a sign of your inadequacy but a sign that you need to choose what to set aside for a while.
overload.practice: Write down everything that's weighing on you, then mark just one thing that truly matters today. Let the rest wait.

unreality.text: Sometimes the world suddenly seems unreal, as if behind glass, and you feel like an observer of your own life. It's a strange and sometimes frightening experience, and it doesn't make you “wrong.” Nussbaum sees emotions as what connects us to the world: through them things become important to us, become “ours.” From her point of view, you could say that when these connections temporarily weaken — from fatigue, stress or pain — the world loses its color and seems flat. In Love's Knowledge she speaks of attentive “perception” of concrete details as a path to reality. The return can begin with something simple: a smell, a sound, a touch that reminds you again that you are here.
unreality.practice: Name five things you can see, four sounds, three sensations in your body. Don't hurry — just notice what is concrete.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. In Upheavals of Thought, Nussbaum singles out a special emotion — wonder. Unlike most feelings, it has almost nothing to do with your personal plans and interests: you are simply struck by the worth of what is before you. Nussbaum believes wonder takes us out of ourselves, widens the circle of what matters to us, and so helps us feel compassion even for distant beings. In Justice for Animals (2023) she writes about how wonder at the lives of animals opens a new world to us. Your awe is a moment when the world showed itself to be larger than you. Stay in it a while.
awe.practice: Try to put into words what exactly struck you. Stay with it for another minute, doing nothing.

relief.text: Relief is a wonderful feeling, and it's worth savoring. From Nussbaum's point of view, relief contains a judgment: the threat to what you care about has passed. It shows how much the thing you were afraid for meant to you. In The Fragility of Goodness, Nussbaum reminds us that much in life is beyond our control, so a good outcome is not only an achievement but also a gift of circumstance. There's no need to go looking straight away for the next reason to worry, or to tell yourself “it's too early to be glad.” Relief is a moment when body and soul can let go of tension. Let yourself live it and perhaps notice who or what helped.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly and notice where in your body the tension has eased. Tell yourself: “Now I can breathe out.”

calm.text: Calm is a valuable state, and you can simply cherish it. Nussbaum wrote a great deal about the Stoics, whose ideal was “apatheia” — freedom from the passions, attachments included. She disagrees with them: a calm bought at the price of refusing to love and value things impoverishes life. From her point of view, you could say there is another kind of calm — not detachment but trust: when you go on caring about people and things, but right now none of them is under threat. Such calm doesn't contradict living feelings; it gives them room. You don't need to do anything with it or fear that it will end. You can simply be in it and notice what it rests on.
calm.practice: Notice what helps you feel calm right now: a place, people, a rhythm. Remember it as one of your resources.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful surge, when you want to create and act. Nussbaum's list of central human capabilities includes “senses, imagination, and thought” — the ability to create, to express yourself and to experience what brings meaning. For her this is not a luxury but part of a life worthy of a human being. In Love's Knowledge she shows that imagination and art are also a way of knowing: they help us see what dry reasoning cannot. From this point of view, inspiration is a moment when your imagination and your values meet. There's no need to check whether it will turn out “good enough.” You can simply follow it and allow yourself the joy of making.
inspiration.practice: Write down the main thought or image right now, while it's alive. Don't edit — just keep it.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is unpleasant to notice in yourself, but almost everyone knows it, and in itself it doesn't make you a bad person. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum describes envy as a feeling that sees the world as a zero-sum game: if the other has gained, I have lost. From this point of view, you could say that schadenfreude is the flip side of envy: someone else's failure seems for a moment to restore the balance. In Anger and Forgiveness, Nussbaum calls this logic “the road of status” — when everything comes down to who is higher and who is lower. Schadenfreude hints at where you feel wounded or undervalued. That is useful knowledge, and you can use it to tend to your own wound rather than to another person's fall.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “What in me was hurt by things going well for this person?” Write down the answer — it's about you, not about them.

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling, and it's awkward to admit. But it often protects something vulnerable. In Hiding from Humanity, Nussbaum shows how people try to put others “beneath” them so as not to feel their own weakness, dependence and imperfection. She describes this mechanism as “projection”: what we don't want to see in ourselves we attribute to others, and then look down on them. In Anger and Forgiveness a similar logic is called “status-lowering.” This doesn't mean your contempt sees nothing: sometimes it is reacting to a real injustice. But it's worth asking what pain it shields you from. You can acknowledge the feeling without turning it into treating a person as lesser.
contempt.practice: Ask yourself: “What of the things I despise in them would I not want to see in myself?” Just note the answer, without condemning yourself.

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong and ancient reaction, and everyone has it. In Hiding from Humanity (2004), Nussbaum distinguishes “primary” disgust — at bodily wastes, decay, rot — from “projective” disgust, which is transferred onto people and groups. In her view, primary disgust is connected with our wish not to be animals, not to be mortal and vulnerable. Projective disgust, she argues, is an unreliable moral guide: it often says more about our fear than about the other person. When disgust is turned on yourself, it too can be a flight from your own bodily nature. The feeling itself is not your fault. What matters is noticing when it becomes the basis for judgments about people.
disgust.practice: When disgust rises, ask yourself: “Is this my body reacting to something specific, or a judgment about a person?” Just tell the one from the other.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and you want justice to be restored. In Anger and Forgiveness, Nussbaum examines this thought in detail. She acknowledges that pain and outrage are justified if you really were harmed. But the idea that the wrongdoer's suffering will fix something she calls “the road of payback” — a kind of magical thinking: the past won't become different, and your wound won't heal from someone else's. Nussbaum proposes “Transition-Anger”: acknowledging that what happened was unacceptable and turning toward the future — toward protecting yourself, toward recovery, toward what can be changed by legitimate means. A fantasy of revenge is a signal of your pain. You can act for yourself rather than against the other.
revenge.practice: Ask yourself: “What do I actually need in order to feel safe and to recover?” Write down one thing that is about you, not about the person who hurt you.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people closest to you is one of the most common human emotions, and it almost always leaves you ashamed afterward. In Anger and Forgiveness, Nussbaum devotes a separate chapter to anger in intimate relationships. She notes that this is exactly where we are most vulnerable: so much depends on those close to us that their actions hurt more. Nussbaum believes that such anger often hides fear and grief, and that “keeping score” — who owes whom what — only pushes people apart. In Upheavals of Thought, following Melanie Klein, she writes that love and aggression toward the same person coexist from childhood, and that maturity lies in striving for “reparation,” for restoring the connection. Your anger does not cancel your love.
anger_at_loved.practice: Ask yourself: “What am I really afraid of, or grieving, when I'm angry at this person?” When you're ready, you can tell them about that rather than about the anger.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is a very common state, and not at all “abnormal.” In Upheavals of Thought, drawing on the psychoanalysts Melanie Klein and Donald Winnicott, Nussbaum writes that ambivalence begins in infancy: the same adult who feeds and comforts sometimes doesn't come and disappoints. The child learns to understand that this is one and the same person — not ideal and not evil, but whole. Nussbaum believes that mature love sees the other as a separate, imperfect person and can hold mixed feelings toward them. From this point of view, your ambivalence is not an absence of love but a sign that you see the person close to you as a whole.
ambivalence.practice: Write two columns about someone close to you: “what I love in them” and “what I find hard to bear.” Notice that both are true at once.

guilty_relief.text: Relief you feel ashamed of is rarely spoken about out loud, yet many people feel it. For example, after leaving a hard job, after a breakup, or after a loved one's long illness. For Nussbaum, emotions are judgments of value, and a person can hold several true judgments at the same time. “I loved him” and “it was unbearably hard for me” — both thoughts are true. In The Fragility of Goodness she shows how different values can conflict, and how an honest life acknowledges that conflict instead of pretending that one of the feelings is wrong. Your relief does not cancel your love and care. It speaks of how long you carried the weight, and of the fact that you too have a right to a life.
guilty_relief.practice: Finish two sentences: “It mattered to me that…” and “It was hard for me that…” Let both remain true.

indifference.text: Sometimes you aren't moved by what you “should” be moved by, and that feels unsettling. In Upheavals of Thought, Nussbaum explains how compassion works: we feel another's misfortune when that person enters our “circle of concern.” This requires what she calls a “eudaimonistic judgment” — a sense that this person matters to my own life. If the connection isn't felt, the feelings stay silent, and that is not a moral failure but a feature of emotions. Besides, indifference can be a defense when the soul is overloaded with pain. Nussbaum believes that imagination — literature, art, particular stories — can gradually widen this circle. Indifference is not a verdict on your ability to feel; it may be a signal of fatigue or distance.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself without reproach: “Am I tired of feeling, or do I simply not see a connection with this?” Either answer is normal.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and leave — to change your job, your city or your role — is common and understandable. It says that your present life is squeezing you somehow. Nussbaum's capabilities approach includes “practical reason” — being able to decide for yourself what your life will be — as well as “play,” “affiliation” and “control over one's environment.” From this point of view, you could say that the wish to escape is a signal: one of these capabilities has no room right now. It's not weakness or irresponsibility, but information. Nussbaum values attentive perception of the particular. Before deciding anything, it helps to understand what exactly you want to get away from, and what you are really drawn toward.
escape.practice: Finish two sentences: “I want to get away from…” and “I want to get to…” The second part often matters more than the first.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is the “wrong” person or unavailable can be embarrassing, frightening and delightful all at once. Nussbaum doesn't pass verdicts here, but she invites us to look closely. In The Fragility of Goodness she examines Plato's dialogue Phaedrus, in which Socrates speaks of the “madness” of love as a force that reveals to us the worth of another person. For Nussbaum, attraction is not just an impulse but a judgment: in this person I see something important. She also writes about “the tragic question” — when different values and commitments collide, and the conflict itself doesn't make a person bad. Understanding what exactly you see in the other and what it says about you matters more than rushing to judgment.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: “What exactly draws me to this person — what value do I see in them?” Write the answer down just for yourself.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and of their judgment is agonizing, and there's nothing shameful in it. In Hiding from Humanity, Nussbaum describes “primitive shame” — the fear that others will see us as imperfect, needy, not the way we are “supposed” to be. She shows that everyone hides their vulnerability, and that the image of the “normal,” flawless person is largely a fiction that society uses to stigmatize those who are different. From this point of view, your shyness is not proof that something is wrong with you, but a heightened form of a feeling everyone has. The people around you are also afraid of being seen. Knowing this can make encounters a little easier.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, try to notice a sign of uncertainty in someone else. Remind yourself: “They're human too, just like me.”

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: it's difficult to live when you don't know what will happen. In The Fragility of Goodness, Nussbaum shows that the ancient Greeks dreamed of conquering tyche — chance — with techne, an art and reason that would control everything. She thinks this dream is understandable but entirely unattainable, and that striving for complete invulnerability impoverishes life: you would have to give up love, friendship and everything that doesn't depend on us. Nussbaum compares a good life to a plant rather than a jewel. Uncertainty is not your failure but the condition of a life that has something living and valuable in it.
uncertainty.practice: Write down one thing that is uncertain right now, and one thing you can lean on whatever happens.

quote.text: Being a good human being is to have a kind of openness to the world, an ability to trust uncertain things beyond your own control… it's based on being more like a plant than like a jewel, something rather fragile, but whose very particular beauty is inseparable from that fragility.
quote.author: Martha Nussbaum
quote.source: Interview with Bill Moyers, A World of Ideas (1988)

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — wears you out: you can no longer influence the outcome, but you don't know it yet. In The Monarchy of Fear, following ancient authors, Nussbaum notes that hope and fear are twins: both are born when something important is out of our hands. While you wait, they take turns, and that is exhausting. Nussbaum doesn't suggest, as the Stoics did, giving up hope so as not to be afraid. She suggests giving hope a place as a practice: go on living, doing things, being with people while there is no answer yet. Your waiting is so hard because the outcome matters to you. That is no reason to put your life on hold until the answer comes.
waiting.practice: For the time of waiting, choose one small activity that is pleasant or useful to you. Do it whenever your thoughts return to the waiting.

regret.text: Everyone knows regret for what they did or didn't do, and it shows that you care. In The Fragility of Goodness, Nussbaum examines Greek tragedy — for example Agamemnon, forced to choose between two terrible options. She believes that in such situations the right response is not unfeelingness but pain that acknowledges the worth of what was lost. Regret, from this point of view, is a way of honestly seeing that the other path had value too. But Nussbaum distinguishes this from self-punishment: in Anger and Forgiveness she warns against “payback,” including payback aimed at oneself. Regret can become respect for what was lost and a lesson for the future, rather than an endless trial of yourself.
regret.practice: Write one sentence: “I regret…, because what mattered to me was…” What does that say about your values today?

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a heavy feeling, and it is full of love. In Upheavals of Thought, Nussbaum argues against the Platonic idea that love should ascend from one person to beauty in general in order to become safer. She defends love for the particular and irreplaceable: this person is not an example of something general, and cannot be replaced by someone “similar.” That is why longing is so specific: what you miss is precisely their voice, their habits, the way they look at you. From this point of view, longing is not weakness but evidence of how precisely you saw and loved the other. There's no need to hurry it: it reflects a bond that remains real even when the person is not near.
longing.practice: Recall one specific detail of this person — a gesture, a phrase, a tone of voice. Stay with that memory for a minute.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from hard news, wars, injustice — shows that your heart is open. In Upheavals of Thought, Nussbaum analyzes compassion: it includes the judgment that another's suffering is serious, that it is undeserved, and that this person matters to you. She considers compassion the foundation of a just society. But in The Monarchy of Fear she warns that when the pain is too great, fear can contract us, turning into powerlessness or anger. As a counterweight she names hope as a practice: small concrete deeds, company, art. You don't have to carry all the world's pain alone. You can feel it and still save your strength to do your own part.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete good deed that is within your reach today — even a very small one. Then give yourself time to rest from the news.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply, and the pain is understandable. From Nussbaum's point of view, you could say that two feelings are often intertwined in it. One is grief: you hoped for a connection, and it won't happen. The other is what she calls in Anger and Forgiveness a “status-injury”: the sense that you were ranked lower, that you are “worse.” Nussbaum believes the second thought is deceptive: your worth as a person is not determined by someone else's choice. The other person is free and separate from you, and their decision speaks of their desires and circumstances, not of your value. The grief is worth living through, but the verdict on yourself you can decline to accept.
rejection.practice: Divide a sheet of paper: “what I lost” and “what I decided about myself.” Ask yourself whether the second is true.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is one of the most ancient fears, and it can be very strong. In The Monarchy of Fear, Nussbaum writes that fear is born of infant helplessness: the infant depends entirely on others, and their absence feels like a threat to life itself. Adults carry this trace. Drawing on the psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott, Nussbaum speaks of “the capacity to be alone” — it develops as a child gradually learns to trust that care will return. From this point of view, your fear is not weakness but the voice of that very early need. As an adult, you can give yourself some of the support that others once gave, and look for reliable people nearby.
abandonment.practice: Place a hand on your chest and tell yourself: “I'm here, I won't abandon myself.” Recall one person who was there for you at a hard moment.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a particular kind of pain: you love, and the other doesn't respond. In Upheavals of Thought, Nussbaum stresses that mature love sees the other as a separate, free person, not an extension of one's own desires. Hence a hard truth: love cannot be earned or compelled. But it doesn't follow that your love is meaningless or that you aren't good enough. For Nussbaum, love is a judgment about another person's worth, and that judgment can be true even when it isn't returned. It's natural to grieve for what didn't come to be, and that takes time you shouldn't rush. But the very capacity to love like this is yours, and it stays with you when this story is over.
unrequited.practice: Write down what you saw of value in this person. And then — what this love told you about what matters to you.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the hardest experiences, especially if it was public. In Hiding from Humanity, Nussbaum examines humiliation in detail and opposes it as a violation of human dignity. She shows that the one who humiliates often projects onto the other their own fear of being weak and imperfect. For Nussbaum, dignity is not something that can be taken from a person: it belongs to them simply because they are human. So humiliation, however painful, says more about the one who inflicted it than about you. Your pain is real and deserves attention. But your dignity has stayed with you, even if at that moment it seemed otherwise.
humiliation.practice: Write to yourself: “What was done to me does not cancel my dignity.” Read it aloud, even if you don't quite believe it yet.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is very common, and there's no need to shame yourself even more for it. In Hiding from Humanity, Nussbaum shows how society transfers disgust at its own animality and mortality onto bodies — especially those that don't fit narrow standards. In Aging Thoughtfully (2017, co-written with Saul Levmore), she writes about how such disgust affects, for example, aging bodies. In her view, these standards are not an objective truth about beauty but largely a projection of a shared fear of being vulnerable. In her approach, the body is not an object to be graded but a source of capabilities: to move, to feel, to take pleasure, to be with others.
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body lets you do or feel. Thank it for one of them.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, it's frightening and unfair, and these feelings are legitimate. In The Fragility of Goodness, Nussbaum shows that a good human life is inevitably vulnerable: it depends on the body, on luck, on circumstances that are not always in our control. This is not your failure. In Hiding from Humanity she writes about how people are ashamed of their neediness and their dependence on others, dreaming of an invulnerability that no one has. Nussbaum, on the contrary, considers dependence part of a normal human life. Accepting help is not humiliating — it is what people have always done for one another. Illness does not cancel your worth or your ability to love and be loved.
illness.practice: Think about what others could help you with right now. Choose one small request and allow yourself to say it.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy and well-earned feeling, and it's worth enjoying. From Nussbaum's point of view, it contains a judgment: I have done something valuable, and it matters to my life. In Anger and Forgiveness she warns against one kind of pride — the kind that puts itself above others and is focused on status. But pride in the work itself is different: it doesn't need anyone to lose. In her capabilities approach, Nussbaum values “practical reason” and the ability to carry out your plans. Your pride is a recognition that you have used these capabilities. Let yourself be glad, without making light of what you've done.
pride.practice: Write down what you did and what it took to make it happen. Tell yourself: “I did this.”

melancholy.text: Melancholy — a bright sadness — is a subtle feeling that holds both sorrow and beauty. In Upheavals of Thought, Nussbaum devotes a whole chapter to music — Mahler in particular — and to how music can express and clarify complex emotions. From her point of view, you could say that melancholy is a quiet acknowledgment of the fragility of everything valuable: you sense that beautiful things are not eternal, and that makes them all the more precious. It's the same thought as in The Fragility of Goodness: the beauty of human life is inseparable from its vulnerability. Melancholy doesn't need to be fixed. You can live through it the way you listen to sad music — letting it reveal something about what you hold dear.
melancholy.practice: Listen to one piece of music that matches your mood. Notice what it says about what you hold dear.
